data.title: College sports bill holding up Senate's path to August recess
data.description:
Senate Republicans say getting consent to move forward on the Protect College Sports Act, a bipartisan bill to set rules for compensating and recruiting college athletes, is holding up a broader deal on funding the government, confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general and starting the five-week Senate recess.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) told GOP colleagues at a lunch meeting Friday that he views the college sports bill — which has been dubbed the “NIL bill” because it would set standards for using athletes name, image and likeness — as the “chokepoint” for getting a deal done to fund the government and start the August recess, according to a source familiar with the internal meeting.

A senior Senate GOP aide confirmed that there’s agreement on voting on everything on Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s (R-S.D.) to-do list but that there are about 10 holds on the college sports bill.

Senate GOP leaders circulated a “hotline” alert on Friday afternoon proposing votes to amend the continuing resolution funding government to strip out a controversial hemp-related provision, to pass the continuing resolution itself, and to confirm Blanche as attorney general, as well as votes on a motion to proceed to the college sports bill.

Under the proposed hotline, the Senate would then vote on the college sports bill itself if the motion to proceed to it is successful.

The proposed list of actions also includes test vote on proceeding to a Senate budget resolution, which is expected to fail, and a vote on a measure sponsored by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) requiring photo identification to vote in federal elections.

Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is pushing hard to vote on the college sports bill before the Senate leaves for a five-week August recess but he’s running into opposition, which could scuttle getting an agreement to sequence the final series of votes before the recess.

Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) said the proposed regulations for college sports are “complicated” and he would be happy to spend more time on the bill before voting on it.

“It’s complicated, there are a lot of pieces to this. I’m okay with waiting,” he said.

Warnock held up action on a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill earlier this week until he got an assurance from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to put some guardrails on President Trump’s expanded tariff authority under the bill.

Thune acknowledged that getting agreement on the college sports bill is an obstacle to wrapping up the Senate’s work before the recess.

“NIL Is an issue that we got to get better clarity on to lock down an agreement. It’s part of the endgame,” Thune said.

data.title: Vance on joke about columnist's weight: 'I feel pretty good about that'
data.description:
Vice President Vance defended his jab about Washington Post columnist and Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen’s weight after the price of a $20 burrito sparked a GOP debate over affordability.

In an interview with Salem News Channel’s Hugh Hewitt, Vance doubled down on his fat joke directed at Thiessen as part of an ongoing online conversation about the current price of food and inflation.

“You know, it was a joke, Hugh. I think there are ways in which you’re allowed to punch back, and you’re allowed to be a little bit humorous,” Vance said. “I’m sure it was not as charitable as I should have been.”

The exchange began earlier this week when Turning Point USA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet shared a college student’s complaint that a “burrito shouldn’t cost $20,” arguing the sentiment reflects broader frustrations among young voters about affordability and cautioned Republicans not to brush this off.

Thiessen pushed back on the complaint on social media, writing, “Cry me a river. The burritos in the college cafeteria are included in your meal plan.”

Vance then jumped into the debate with a joke about Thiessen’s weight.

“I’m surprised to hear Mark say this,” Vance wrote, misspelling Thiessen’s first name. “If you’ve ever met him in person, it’s quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito.”

Hewitt asked Vance on Thursday whether he regretted “taking a punch at a fellow Catholic,” while interviewing the vice president about his new book on his conversion to Catholicism.

Vance conceded that his comment may have fallen short of the standards of the Catholic faith, but did not express regret.

“I certainly wish him the best. I think he’s been a little unfair to me over the last couple of weeks, and so I decided to hit back with a little spice,” Vance said of Thiessen.

Vance said he looked to Jesus Christ as an example, pointing to Jesus’ humility and “remarkable way with words.”

“I’m always going to fall short of that example, but I don’t think that there’s anything wrong with being a little spicy from time to time,” he said. “Right now I feel pretty good about that.”

The $20 burrito discussion grew into a wider debate over how Republicans should talk about affordability.

Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) faced backlash after pushing back on complaints about the current cost of food, telling young people to live on a budget with roommates as previous generations did.

“The market doesn’t care what you think something ‘should’ cost,” Crenshaw wrote on social media.

He later sarcastically apologized for “triggering the comment section,” after taking heat online before doubling down and pushing back on whether conservatives should abandon their free-market principles to appeal to voters.

data.title: Agriculture groups call on Senate to pass reconciliation in White House push
data.description:
The White House is amplifying calls from agricultural associations for the Senate to pass a $95 billion framework for a third budget reconciliation package, which includes a tranche of farm aid along with emergency Iran war funding.

In statements first provided to The Hill by the White House, the American Sugar Alliance, the Farm Credit Council, the Forest Landowners Association, and the National Cotton Council all called on the Senate to pass the package. 

The $95 billion framework, which was passed in the House last month, provides $12 billion in agriculture aid, along with $73 billion in defense and intelligence funding, and $10 billion for a fund aimed at incentivizing states to adopt Trump-backed voting restrictions. 

“Farm Credit thanks the Senate for consideration of a reconciliation package that includes $12 billion in critical economic and disaster assistance for farmers, ranchers and rural communities,” said Christy Seyfert, president and CEO and the Farm Credit Council, urging “swift passage” of the legislation. 

A spokesperson for the Forest Landowners Association also cited the importance of providing disaster relief as a part of passing the package, noting the uptick in wildfires and hurricane season.

“Congress and the Administration must ensure disaster relief funding and recovery opportunities are readily available so private forest landowners can restore damaged forests and continue keeping America’s working forests healthy, productive, and resilient,” the spokesperson said. 

The American Sugar Alliance’s executive committee noted how the agricultural and tax provisions of last year’s reconciliation package help with “meaningful progress” toward helping producers “weather those economic headwinds.” 

“We commend Congress for recognizing the need to strengthen the farm safety net and provide tax policies that support family farming operations and rural businesses,” the committee said. 

The National Cotton Council called on the Senate Agriculture Committee to pass a package that “at least mirrors the $12 billion of the House directive – or, ideally, slightly exceeds it.”

The package faces an uphill climb in the upper chamber.

Senate Republicans are divided over the package, which includes financial incentives for passing election laws including the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-N.D.) has repeatedly said that Republicans do not have the votes to pass the SAVE Act.

Additionally, Republicans remain divided over the amount of funds in the package, while some are wary of funding an unpopular war. The White House argues the funds are necessary to replenish U.S. stockpiles of modern weapons and ensure future military innovation.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly touted the Trump administration’s record on agriculture in a statement to The Hill and pledged  that the legislation would “strengthen our rural economy.” 

“President Trump has done more for American agriculture than anyone by negotiating new trade deals, expanding foreign market access, lowering input costs, bolstering the farm safety net, doubling the death tax exemption, ending taxes on rural property loan interest, creating rural opportunity zones, and more,” Kelly said.

data.title: Trump response to Pirro question 'shocking': Haberman
data.description:
Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for The New York Times, called President Trump’s public criticism of U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro over her handling of the Reflecting Pool vandalism case “shocking” on Thursday. 

The president said in a Saturday post on Truth Social that he disagreed “100%” with Pirro’s decision to dismiss felony charges against Olympic canoeist David Hearn.

The U.S. attorney made the decision after prosecutors found that the damage to the pool was not due to vandalism but rather a product of flawed renovation work commissioned by the White House. 

Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that Pirro “choked” and said the judge overseeing the case was “extremely unfriendly” to the U.S. attorney. He later added that Pirro “folded like an umbrella.”

Haberman said the president “looked visibly angry” in his comments to reporters following Pirro’s decision to drop these charges. 

“I think that for Pirro, who has always believed that he would be very loyal to her because she has been very loyal to him, it was pretty surprising,” Haberman told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins. “It probably shouldn’t have been.”

The Justice Department on Monday dropped charges against three additional people accused of vandalizing the iconic landmark. Hearn and the three others were accused of destruction of property with a value of less than $1,000. 

Hearn was indicted by a grand jury in Washington last month on charges of felony destruction of property and faced 10 years in prison. A local judge formally dismissed the vandalism charge against Hearn on Thursday. 

Hearn told Collins on “The Source with Kaitlan Collins” on Thursday evening he was feeling “a bit relieved now that the case has been dismissed officially.”

“But I’m still pretty concerned about innocent people being accused by the government of things they didn’t do,” he added. “It’s a really unsettling feeling for me.”

data.title: ICE body camera releases must be in agency's 'best interests': Policy
data.description:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will equip its officers with body cameras over the next two months, according to reports, but the agency’s policy gives officials broad discretion over footage released to the public that’s deemed in its “best interests.” 

More than half of the agency’s field officers have already been outfitted with the body cams, according to The Associated Press. The others are expected to receive them by the end of September.

The rollout follows increased pressure and public scrutiny on the agency after fatal shootings involving ICE officers amid President Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration, leading lawmakers to call on the agency for more transparency.

Under an ICE directive issued in February 2025, officers are required to activate their cameras at the beginning of enforcement activities, including arrests, stops and searches.

If the footage captures an incident involving serious bodily injury or death while in custody, the agency said it will review the video and release it to the public — but only if the administration determines doing so is “in the best interests of the agency.”

While the agency generally aims to complete that process within 72 hours, the director can withhold or indefinitely delay its release if there are “specific and compelling circumstances” against releasing it that cannot be solved through redactions.

A review group consisting of senior ICE officials, lawyers and other agency personnel will look through the recordings of serious incidents and issue recommendations to leadership about whether a public release is warranted.

The policy also requires ICE to redact officers’ faces and other identifying information before releasing it.

In July, an ICE officer fatally shot a 25-year-old motorist in Maine, and in a separate incident another officer shot and killed a homebuilder driving to work in Houston. Neither encounter was recorded on an officer body camera.

White House border czar Tom Homan said last month that body cameras would provide more transparency into confrontations involving immigration officers.

“I think body cameras are the way to go,” he told CBS News’ Margaret Brennan at the time. “I think body cameras let the American people know what that officer sees when he takes that action.”

data.title: Scientists extend instrument life on Voyager 2 probe
data.description:
(NewsNation) — NASA has extended the life of Voyager 2 after freeing up power from the space probe’s dwindling power supply.

The effort was nicknamed the “Big Bang” by scientists with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who worked to turn off certain powered devices and substitute them with lower-power alternatives while ensuring the spacecraft is still warm enough to operate.

Launched in 1977, Voyager 2 was dispatched to study the outer planets of the solar system. Along with its sister craft, Voyager 1, the probe is now traveling through interstellar space.

Both Voyagers are powered by devices that convert heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. As the plutonium supply depletes, the probes lose about four watts of power per year. Nearly 50 years after launch, the power margins have grown thin, the team shutting off non-essential systems to conserve energy.

Two of Voyager 2’s instruments had previously been turned off due to lower power. Prior to the Big Bang solution, the mission would have had to shut off another instrument by the end of the year.

Now, the probe’s three instruments should be able to continue operating for at least one extra year.

There are plans to perform the same swap on Voyager 1 in coming months.

data.title: Senate confirms FEMA leader
data.description:
The Senate has confirmed President Trump’s pick to lead the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), which has faced significant scrutiny for its handling of disasters and funding under the Trump administration.

The Senate approved the nomination of Cameron Hamilton to lead the agency as part of a larger slate of 74 nominations confirmed together as a block in a 51-47 vote.

Also confirmed in the vote was Hal Duncan, who will be the deputy director of the White House Office of Management and Budget.

Hamilton previously served as FEMA’s acting leader at the start of the Trump administration, but he was ousted after saying that the agency should not be eliminated, contradicting Trump and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

He was nominated to lead the disaster response agency after Noem’s departure earlier this year.

In his confirmation hearing, Hamilton said that FEMA should seek to “strike a new balance” that encourages cost savings.

“I think many states and local officials have had incentives to drive up costs,” he said. 

“Yes, they’re entitled to support. We, as the agency, have confirmed we would need to strike a new balance to encourage cost reasonableness and cost savings,” he added.

However, he also backed away from an idea he floated last year that would have quadrupled the threshold for states to qualify for a major disaster declaration and attached federal assistance. 

As the Trump administration has moved away from calling for shuttering FEMA outright, the president and other leaders have indicated that they want to dole out less assistance to states.

Developing…

data.title: Watch live: Trump hosts roundtable on mining
data.description:
President Trump on Friday afternoon will host a roundtable at the State Department centered on the mining industry.

“The mining industry has never had a greater champion than President Trump,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement. “His unprecedented support has driven record investment, streamlined permitting, and delivered real results for American workers, companies, and communities.”

She added, “President Trump is the first president in decades to prioritize our country’s mining industry, unleash its abundant resources, and build the next generation of American miners.”

He is also expected to announce $180 million in grant funding to boost education around mining, according to White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

Trump will be joined by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and a group of industry experts.

The event is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: Dr. Oz urges senators to reject Budd hemp amendment
data.description:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), is urging senators to not support an amendment that would allow a federal ban on most hemp-derived products to take effect in November.

In a Friday letter, Oz noted he had “grave concerns” about the amendment from Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) that would strip from a government funding bill a one-month delay of the ban. 

“Passage of this amendment would undo significant gains that have been made to make clinically-appropriate full-spectrum hemp-derived CBD accessible to the senior citizens and individuals with disabilities that rely on the Medicare program for their healthcare,” the CMS chief wrote. 

The Trump administration earlier this year launched a pilot program that would allow Medicare providers that participate in select programs to offer eligible hemp products to eligible beneficiaries. 

Participants may provide up to $500 worth of hemp products annually. Medicare itself will not reimburse providers for the products, however, so participating organizations bear the costs.  

The administration highlighted the availability of full-spectrum CBD, which contains all of the compounds found in the cannabis plant including trace amounts of THC that are not enough to produce a psychoactive effect. 

But the program encompasses all hemp-derived products containing no more than 0.3 percent delta-9 THC by total weight; the same definition of hemp included in the 2018 Farm Bill. CMS said it would change the requirements if hemp laws changed.  

Oz in the letter said passage of the amendment would “rip away from millions of seniors and disabled Americans the opportunity to benefit from these new programs.” 

The underlying spending bill would also delay the restrictions on intoxicating hemp products enacted last year until December, though cannabinoids that cannot naturally be produced by the cannabis plant would still lose their federal hemp status on November 12. 

Hemp industry stakeholders say the extra month will give them additional time to convince lawmakers that regulation, not prohibition, is the best path forward.   

The provision was inserted into the bill at the behest of the White House, though it has bipartisan backing. Budd’s amendment would strip that delay from the bill.  

Budd and other co-sponsors of the amendment are slowing consideration of the spending bill until they can get a vote. There are currently 13 co-sponsors. 

The senators say they are trying to protect children from illicit products that are intentionally marketed to children.  

The products are labeled as hemp, but contain extremely high levels of synthetic THC, the psychedelic compound in marijuana responsible for a high.   

Oz said the administration shares the same goals and is “focused on preventing dangerous products from reaching Americans.

“You each have my commitment to continue to work with you on meeting our shared goals of ensuring patient access and protection of the public health,” he wrote.
